narrative: During the 1930s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were characterized by a rich diversity of traditional styles that celebrated their natural textures and cultural heritage. The afro, which was created by combing out kinky hair or using chemical curling products, became a signature style for many women. Cornrows, a traditional three-strand braid originating from Africa, were also popular among Black and African women as a protective hairstyle that minimized manipulation and exposure to environmental elements. Dreadlocks, made of rope-like strands of hair, could form naturally in very curly or kinky hair, while box braids, a type of protective style, consisted of square-shaped hair divisions that added thickness and versatility to the natural hair. Although documentation from this era is limited, it is clear that these hairstyles were not only aesthetically pleasing but also deeply rooted in African identity and culture. As such, they played a significant role in shaping the self-expression and empowerment of Black and African women during this time period.
